title: AI agent
description: How the Codexa agent plans, edits files with tools, validates in the sandbox, repairs errors, and how every run can be reviewed and reverted.
category: Build
order: 12
tags: [ai, agent, tools, repair, snapshots]
author: Codexa Team
date: 2026-10-24
related: [prompting, projects, troubleshooting]
---

The agent is a bounded, tool-using loop that works on the real files in your project. It never runs code inside Codexa's web server: anything that executes (installs, builds, tests) happens in the project's isolated sandbox through the runner service.

## Providers and configuration

Codexa has a provider abstraction with adapters for **Anthropic** and **OpenAI** models. The operator of a deployment configures an API key and a default provider/model; the agent panel shows which one is active. When no key is configured, the panel renders an explicit **not configured** state and `POST .../ai/generate` returns `ai_not_configured` instead of pretending to work.

Workspace-level connections for OpenAI and Anthropic (under Integrations) are stored encrypted and tested with a lightweight request when you add them.

## Modes

| Mode  | Tools available                         | Use it for                                        |
| ----- | --------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- |
| Build | read, search, run commands, write, edit, delete, finish | New features and changes                 |
| Ask   | read, search, run commands              | Questions about the code; nothing is written      |
| Fix   | same as Build, with a repair-oriented prompt | Pasted errors and failing builds             |

## Stages of a run

Every run streams its progress as events (`stage`, `text`, `tool_call`, `tool_result`, `file_change`, `plan`, `usage`, `done`, `error`) over a server-sent-events connection. The stages are:

1. **queued** – the run row is created and your message is stored.
2. **loading_context** – the file tree, the most relevant files and the last ten messages of the conversation are gathered. Tool outputs are truncated to safe sizes and never include environment variable values.
3. **planning** – the model is given a single `propose_plan` tool and returns a short plan, shown in the panel.
4. **working** – the model calls tools in a loop. Before the first write a snapshot named `Before AI run <id>` is created.
5. **validating** – the agent runs allow-listed commands in the sandbox (`typecheck`, `build`, `test`) and reads the output.
6. **repairing** – if validation fails, the agent is shown the errors and tries again, at most **two** repair attempts.
7. **done** – the run ends as `succeeded`, `failed` or `cancelled`, with token usage recorded.

## Tools

The agent's tools are deliberately small:

- `list_files`, `read_file`, `search_files` – read access to the stored project files.
- `write_file`, `edit_file`, `delete_file` – changes, recorded as file changes on the run.
- `run_command` – one of `install`, `build`, `test`, `typecheck` in the sandbox. Arbitrary shell is not available.
- `get_logs` – recent runtime logs.
- `propose_plan`, `finish` – structure the run.

Paths are validated so the agent cannot read or write outside the project.

## Limits

| Limit                           | Value                       |
| ------------------------------- | --------------------------- |
| Prompt length                   | 8,000 characters            |
| Tool calls per run              | 40                          |
| Model turns per run             | 60                          |
| Wall-clock time per run         | 25 minutes                  |
| Output tokens per model call    | 16,000                      |
| Repair attempts                 | 2                           |
| Provider retries on transient errors | 2                      |

Runs also count against the workspace's monthly AI request and token quotas. When a quota is exhausted the run is refused with `quota_exceeded` (HTTP 402) before anything is sent to the provider.

## Review and revert

Each run links to the snapshot taken before it and to the list of files it changed.

- **Review** opens a per-file diff between that snapshot and the current files.
- **Revert** restores the snapshot. Changes you made by hand after the run are included in the revert, so review first.
- **Cancel** stops a running run at the next tool boundary; files already written stay, and the snapshot still lets you revert.

## Conversations

Conversations group messages per project. Only the last ten messages are sent as history, so long conversations do not grow the context without bound. Start a new conversation when you change topic.

## What the agent cannot do

- Deploy, change billing, invite members or touch workspace settings.
- Reach the network from the sandbox beyond what the sandbox policy allows for package installs.
- Read environment variable values; it sees names only.
- Run outside the sandbox's CPU, memory, process and time limits.

title: Authentication
description: Adding authentication to generated applications, and how Codexa's own accounts, sessions and verification work.
category: Build
order: 14
tags: [authentication, sessions, security]
author: Codexa Team
date: 2026-10-24
related: [security, databases, environment-variables]

This page covers two different things: how to add sign-in to an app you build with Codexa, and how Codexa authenticates *you*.

## Adding auth to a generated app

Codexa's templates do not ship with authentication; you add it with the agent or by hand. The approach depends on the template:

### Node + Express API

Session or token based auth lives in the API. A realistic prompt:

```text
Add email/password authentication:
- POST /auth/signup and /auth/login with bcrypt-hashed passwords stored in
  the users table (see schema below)
- httpOnly session cookie, 7-day expiry, sessions table
- a requireUser middleware used by every /api route
- no new dependencies other than bcrypt and cookie-parser
```

Store the session secret and database URL as [environment variables](/docs/environment-variables), never in code.

### Vite + React single-page app

A browser app has no secrets. Either:

- pair it with a Node + Express project that owns sessions and expose `/api/me`, or
- use a hosted auth provider (Supabase Auth is a common choice when you already connected Supabase) and keep only the public key in the client.

### Static sites

Static hosting serves files; there is no server to check a session. Put anything that needs auth behind an API project.

> Tip: Ask the agent in **Ask** mode to explain the trade-offs for your project before building. It reads your actual files.

## How Codexa authenticates you

- **Accounts** are email + password. Passwords are hashed with a modern password hash; plaintext is never stored or logged.
- **Sessions** are httpOnly, `SameSite=Lax` cookies. The token in the cookie is random and only its hash is stored, so a database leak does not yield usable sessions. Sessions expire and can be revoked from account settings.
- **Email verification** uses single-use, expiring tokens, also stored hashed. The same mechanism backs password reset; an invalid or expired link returns `invalid_token`.
- **GitHub sign-in** is available when the operator configures a GitHub OAuth app. It links a GitHub identity to an account; repository access is a separate, explicit step.
- **API access** uses the same session cookie. Personal API tokens are planned; see [API authentication](/api/authentication).
- **Rate limits** apply to sign-up, sign-in, password reset and AI endpoints (`rate_limited`, HTTP 429 with `Retry-After`).

Server code checks authorization on every request with workspace roles; nothing is trusted from the client. See [Security](/docs/security).

title: Billing
description: Plans, currencies, usage limits, how limits are enforced, invoices, payment providers and cancellation.
category: Account

author: Codexa Team
date: 2026-10-24

Billing is per workspace. The plan sets limits that the server enforces; the pricing page shows the current prices in INR and USD with monthly and annual intervals.

## Plans

| Plan       | Projects | Members | AI requests / month | Runtime / month | Deployments / month | Storage |
| ---------- | -------- | ------- | ------------------- | --------------- | ------------------- | ------- |
| Free       | 3        | 1       | 50                  | 5 hours         | 5                   | 250 MB  |
| Pro        | 25       | 1       | 1,000               | 100 hours       | 100                 | 5 GB    |
| Team       | 100      | 10      | 5,000               | 500 hours       | 500                 | 25 GB   |
| Enterprise | custom   | custom  | custom              | custom          | custom              | custom  |

AI tokens are also metered (500k on Free, 10M on Pro, 50M on Team). The full matrix is on [compare plans](/pricing/compare-plans); the values on this page are copied from the plan configuration and may be updated there.

## How limits are enforced

Every metered action (an AI run, a runtime minute, a deployment, a file write that grows storage, a new project or member) is checked **on the server before it happens**. When a limit is reached the API returns HTTP 402 with:

```json
{ "error": { "code": "quota_exceeded", "message": "Usage limit reached for ai requests (50/50). Upgrade your plan to continue.", "details": { "kind": "ai_request", "used": 50, "limit": 50 } } }
```

Counters reset at the start of each calendar month (UTC). Usage is visible under Workspace → Usage and through `GET /api/v1/workspaces/:id/usage`.

## Payment providers

- **Stripe** handles international cards and invoices in USD.
- **Razorpay** handles payments in INR for customers in India.

The checkout endpoint returns a Stripe Checkout URL or a Razorpay order depending on the currency you pick. Subscription state is updated from provider webhooks, which are verified and idempotent (see [Webhooks](/api/webhooks)). If the operator has not configured a provider, the billing page shows it as unavailable rather than failing at checkout.

## Invoices

Invoices come from the provider (Stripe or Razorpay) and are listed on the workspace billing page with links to the provider-hosted PDF.

## Changing or cancelling

- Upgrades take effect immediately; the provider prorates according to its rules.
- Cancelling keeps the paid plan until the end of the current period, then returns the workspace to Free. Projects above the Free limit are kept but new ones cannot be created until you are under the limit.
- Stripe customers can also manage payment methods through the billing portal link.

## Enterprise

Enterprise plans have custom limits and invoice billing. Use [contact sales](/contact-sales).

> Review: Refund terms are described on the [refund policy](/refund-policy) page, which requires legal review before publication.

title: Custom domains
description: Pointing your own domain at a Codexa hosting deployment with a CNAME record, and what is planned for verification.
category: Ship
order: 21
tags: [domains, dns, hosting]
author: Codexa Team
date: 2026-10-24
related: [deployment, billing]
---

Custom domains are available on Pro and Team plans (3 and 20 domains per workspace) for projects deployed with Codexa hosting.

## Current state

Today custom domains are set up **manually with a CNAME record**. Automatic DNS verification and certificate issuance are planned and listed on the [roadmap](/roadmap); until then the steps below are what works.

## Steps

1. Deploy the project with Codexa hosting and note its subdomain (for example `my-site.apps.example.com`).
2. In the project's **Settings → Domains**, add your domain (`www.yourdomain.com`). Codexa records it against the project.
3. At your DNS provider, create a CNAME record:

   | Type  | Name  | Value                          |
   | ----- | ----- | ------------------------------ |
   | CNAME | `www` | `my-site.apps.example.com`     |

4. Wait for DNS to propagate (minutes to a few hours depending on your provider's TTL).
5. Open `https://www.yourdomain.com`. The hosting proxy routes requests by hostname to the project's live deployment.

## Apex domains

Many DNS providers do not allow a CNAME on the apex (`yourdomain.com`). Use your provider's ALIAS/ANAME record if it has one, or redirect the apex to `www` at the provider.

## TLS certificates

Certificates for custom domains depend on the operator's edge configuration. Until automatic issuance ships, ask the operator of your Codexa deployment how certificates are provided for custom hostnames.

## Removing a domain

Remove it from project settings and delete the CNAME record. Requests for a removed hostname return 404 from the hosting proxy.

title: Databases
description: Connecting PostgreSQL and Supabase to a project, browsing the schema, running SQL safely, and using the connection from generated code.
category: Build
order: 13
tags: [database, postgresql, supabase, sql]
author: Codexa Team
date: 2026-10-24
related: [environment-variables, integrations, authentication]
---

Codexa does not host databases. You connect an existing **PostgreSQL** server or a **Supabase** project, and Codexa gives you a schema browser and a SQL runner inside the project, plus the connection string as an environment variable for your code.

## Add a connection

1. Open the project's **Database** panel and choose **Add connection**.
2. Pick PostgreSQL or Supabase. For Supabase, use the connection string from the project's database settings (the pooled "transaction" URL works for serverless-style apps).
3. Paste the connection string. It is encrypted before storage and never returned to the browser again.
4. **Test** performs a `SELECT 1` and reports success or the driver's error message.

Connections are workspace resources; admins manage them under Integrations and any project in the workspace can use them.

## Schema browser

The panel lists schemas, tables, columns with types and nullability, primary keys and indexes, read live from `information_schema`. It is read-only.

## SQL runner

Type a statement and run it. Results show rows, fields and the row count, capped at 500 rows per query.

> Warning: Statements that modify or destroy data (`INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`, `DROP`, `TRUNCATE`, `ALTER`) require a confirmation step. The first request returns `confirmation_required`; the panel shows the statement again and asks you to confirm before it is re-sent with the confirmation flag.

The runner uses the credentials of the connection, so whatever that role can do, the runner can do. Use a least-privilege role for day-to-day work.

## Using the database from your code

Codexa injects nothing automatically. Add an environment variable (for example `DATABASE_URL`) in the project's [environment variables](/docs/environment-variables) and read it from your code. For a Node + Express template:

```ts
import pg from "pg";

const pool = new pg.Pool({ connectionString: process.env.DATABASE_URL });

app.get("/api/orders", async (_req, res) => {
  const { rows } = await pool.query("select id, total from orders order by id desc limit 50");
  res.json(rows);
});
```

For a Vite + React single-page app there is no server, so the browser must not hold database credentials. Either add a Node + Express project as the API, or use Supabase's row-level security with the public anon key.

## Migrations

Codexa does not run migrations for you. Keep migration files in the project (the Node template ships with a `migrations/` folder and an npm script) and run them with **Run command → build/test** or from your own machine.

## Asking the agent

The agent can read your connection *names* and the schema browser output you paste, but it has no tool to query the database. Paste the relevant `CREATE TABLE` statements into the prompt when you ask for code that touches them.

title: Deployment
description: Deploying with Codexa hosting and Vercel, which frameworks are supported, build logs, history and rollback.
category: Ship
order: 20
tags: [deployment, hosting, vercel, rollback]
author: Codexa Team
date: 2026-10-24
related: [custom-domains, environment-variables, troubleshooting]
---

A deployment builds the project in a sandbox and publishes the output. Codexa ships one provider that works out of the box and one adapter that needs a token.

## Providers

| Provider        | Status                        | What it does                                                                 |
| --------------- | ----------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Codexa hosting  | Available                     | Builds in the sandbox and serves the static output at a subdomain with history and rollback. |
| Vercel          | Adapter exists; needs a token | Uploads the build to Vercel through its API using a workspace Vercel connection. Not yet verified end-to-end against real accounts; the panel says so. |

## Supported frameworks

| Template family        | Codexa hosting | Vercel adapter | Notes                                           |
| ---------------------- | -------------- | -------------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
| React + Vite + TS      | Yes            | Yes            | `npm run build` → `dist/`                       |
| Static HTML/CSS/JS     | Yes            | Yes            | No build step; the project root is served       |
| Node + Express API     | No             | No             | Needs a long-running process; run it in a preview or host it elsewhere for now |
| Next.js                | Not yet        | Not yet        | A Next.js template is on the roadmap            |

Codexa hosting is **static** hosting: it serves files, not server processes. Deploy the API part of a project to a Node host and point the frontend at it with an environment variable.

## Deploying with Codexa hosting

1. Open the **Deploy** panel and choose Codexa hosting.
2. The build runs in a fresh sandbox: dependencies are installed, the template's build command runs, and the output directory is captured. The build log streams into the panel.
3. On success the deployment becomes **live** at the project's subdomain. The hostname pattern is set by the operator (for example `<project>.apps.example.com`).
4. Each deployment keeps its build log and output. **Rollback** on any earlier successful deployment makes it live again without rebuilding.

Failed builds never replace the live deployment.

## Deploying with Vercel

1. Add a Vercel connection with a token under workspace Integrations.
2. Choose Vercel in the Deploy panel. Codexa uploads the project files and your environment variables and creates the deployment through the Vercel API.
3. Status and the Vercel URL are polled and shown in the panel.

Without a token the panel renders a **not configured** state with instructions instead of a disabled button.

## Limits

Deployments per month are metered by plan (5 on Free, 100 on Pro, 500 on Team). Exceeding the limit returns `quota_exceeded`.

## Custom domains

Pointing your own domain at a Codexa hosting deployment is done with a CNAME record; see [Custom domains](/docs/custom-domains).

title: Editor
description: The Monaco-based editor - tabs, explorer, search and replace, diagnostics, diff view, autosave and keyboard shortcuts.
category: Build
order: 11
tags: [editor, shortcuts, monaco]

date: 2026-10-24

---

Codexa's editor is built on Monaco, the editor component from VS Code, served from Codexa itself (never from a third-party CDN). It edits the files stored in your project; a running sandbox receives the saved content.

## Layout

- **File explorer** on the left: create, rename, move and delete files and folders. Dragging a file onto a folder moves it.
- **Tabs** across the top of the editor. Unsaved tabs show a dot; middle-click or `Ctrl/Cmd+W` closes a tab.
- **Panels** on the right or bottom: agent chat, preview, logs, history, deploy, database and GitHub. Panels are resizable and remember their size per browser.

## Saving

- `Ctrl/Cmd+S` saves the active file immediately.
- Autosave writes the file about a second after you stop typing. If a save fails (network, permission, quota) the tab keeps its unsaved marker and an error toast explains why.
- Viewers can open files but cannot save; the editor is read-only for them.

## Search and replace

- `Ctrl/Cmd+F` searches inside the open file; `Ctrl/Cmd+H` opens replace.
- `Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+F` searches across every file in the project (server-side, over stored files). Results show path, line and the matching text; clicking one opens the file at that line.
- `Ctrl/Cmd+P` is quick open: type part of a path to jump to a file.

## Diagnostics

TypeScript, JavaScript, JSON and CSS get in-editor diagnostics from Monaco's language services (syntax errors and basic type information). The authoritative check is still the sandbox: **Run type-check** in the Logs panel executes `tsc` against the real dependencies and reports the full output.

## Diff view

The History panel opens any snapshot in a side-by-side diff against the current file. AI runs open the same view, scoped to the files the run changed. The diff is read-only; make edits in the normal tab.

## Keyboard shortcuts

| Shortcut                | Action                                     |
| ----------------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| `Ctrl/Cmd+S`            | Save the active file                       |
| `Ctrl/Cmd+P`            | Quick open a file by path                  |
| `Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+F`      | Search across all files                    |
| `Ctrl/Cmd+F`            | Find in file                               |
| `Ctrl/Cmd+H`            | Find and replace in file                   |
| `Ctrl/Cmd+W`            | Close tab                                  |
| `Ctrl/Cmd+K`            | Open site search (outside the editor)      |
| `Ctrl/Cmd+/`            | Toggle line comment                        |
| `Alt+Up` / `Alt+Down`   | Move line up / down                        |
| `Shift+Alt+F`           | Format document (for languages Monaco supports) |
| `F8`                    | Jump to next diagnostic                    |

Monaco's standard shortcuts (multi-cursor, column select, go to line with `Ctrl/Cmd+G`) all work as in VS Code.

## Languages

Syntax highlighting and basic diagnostics are available for TypeScript, JavaScript, JSX/TSX, JSON, HTML, CSS, Markdown, YAML, SQL and shell. Other files open as plain text.

## Limits

- Files larger than a few megabytes open read-only to keep the browser responsive.
- Monaco needs a modern browser; see [browser support](/browser-support).

title: Environment variables
description: Managing secrets for previews, builds and deployments; how values are encrypted, masked and injected.
category: Build
order: 16
tags: [environment, secrets, configuration]
author: Codexa Team
date: 2026-10-24
related: [security, deployment, databases]
---

Project environment variables hold configuration and secrets your code reads with `process.env.NAME` (or `import.meta.env.VITE_NAME` in Vite apps).

## Managing variables

Open the project's **Settings → Environment variables**.

- Add a variable with a name (`[A-Z_][A-Z0-9_]*`) and a value.
- Values are **encrypted at rest** with the platform encryption key. The list shows masked values; editors and above can reveal a value explicitly, and the reveal is recorded in activity.
- Viewers never see values, masked or not.
- Deleting a variable removes it from the next runtime start and build.

## Where values are injected

| Surface                 | Injected? | Notes                                                   |
| ----------------------- | --------- | ------------------------------------------------------- |
| Preview runtime         | Yes       | Set when the sandbox starts; restart after changes.     |
| Builds for deployment   | Yes       | Available to the build command.                         |
| Codexa static hosting   | No        | Static output has no server; only build-time values exist. |
| Vercel deployments      | Yes       | Sent through the Vercel API with the deployment.        |
| The AI agent            | Names only| The agent sees variable names in context, never values. |

## Vite apps

Vite only exposes variables prefixed with `VITE_` to browser code, and anything exposed that way ends up in the public bundle. Keep real secrets in a server project.

## Node + Express apps

All variables are available as `process.env.*`. Read them once at startup and fail fast when a required one is missing:

```ts
const required = ["DATABASE_URL", "SESSION_SECRET"] as const;
for (const name of required) {
  if (!process.env[name]) throw new Error(`Missing environment variable ${name}`);
}
```

## Duplicating projects

Duplicating a project copies variable **names** with empty values, so you remember what to set without leaking secrets between projects.

## Operator configuration

Platform-level settings (AI keys, OAuth apps, payment and email providers, the runner) are environment variables on the Codexa server itself, not project variables. The product shows explicit "not configured" states when they are absent.

title: Getting started
description: Create a Codexa account, set up your workspace and understand the pieces you will use every day.
category: Start here
order: 1
tags: [account, workspace, basics]
author: Codexa Team
date: 2026-10-24
related: [quickstart, projects, prompting]
---

Codexa turns a written description into a working project, then gives you a real editor, an isolated runtime with a live preview, and a deployment pipeline for the result. This page covers the account and workspace basics; the [quickstart](/docs/quickstart) takes you from a prompt to a running preview.

## Create an account

1. Open [/signup](/signup) and register with an email address and a password (at least 8 characters).
2. Check your inbox for the verification email and open the link. Until the address is verified, actions that send email or create deployments are limited.
3. If the operator has configured GitHub sign-in, a **Continue with GitHub** button appears on the sign-in page. It links a GitHub identity to the same kind of account; nothing about your repositories is read until you explicitly import one.

> Note: Verification emails are sent through a transactional email provider that the operator configures. If the deployment you are using has no email provider, the sign-up page says so and the operator can verify accounts manually.

## Workspaces

Every account gets a **personal workspace**. Projects, usage counters, billing and integrations are attached to a workspace, not to a user.

Team plans add **team workspaces** with four roles:

| Role   | Can do                                                                          |
| ------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Viewer | Open projects, read files, watch previews and logs.                             |
| Editor | Everything a viewer can, plus edit files, run the agent, start runtimes, deploy. |
| Admin  | Everything an editor can, plus invite and remove members, manage integrations.  |
| Owner  | Everything an admin can, plus billing and deleting the workspace.               |

Invitations are sent by email and expire; the invitee must sign in (or sign up) with the invited address.

## What is in a project

A project is a set of files stored in Codexa's database plus everything that happens to them:

- **Files** – ordinary source files. You can download them, push them to GitHub or copy them elsewhere at any time.
- **Snapshots** – named checkpoints with per-file diffs. The agent takes one automatically before every run.
- **Activity** – a log of saves, snapshots, runs and deployments with who did what.
- **Environment variables** – encrypted at rest, injected into previews and builds, never shown to viewers.
- **Deployments** – build history with rollback.

See [Projects](/docs/projects) for the details.

## The three surfaces

- **Editor** – a Monaco-based editor with tabs, file explorer, search and replace, diagnostics and diff view. [Editor docs](/docs/editor).
- **Agent panel** – the chat where you describe changes. The agent plans, edits real files and validates in the sandbox. [AI agent docs](/docs/ai-agent).
- **Preview** – your project running in an isolated sandbox, proxied to a preview URL with streamed logs. [Deployment docs](/docs/deployment) explain how a preview becomes a public site.

## Next steps

- Follow the [quickstart](/docs/quickstart).
- Read the [prompting guide](/docs/prompting) before your first large request; it saves tokens and rework.
- Check [billing](/docs/billing) to understand the Free plan limits.

title: GitHub
description: Connecting GitHub, importing a repository into a project, and committing and pushing project files back.
category: Ship
order: 22
tags: [github, git, import, push]
author: Codexa Team
date: 2026-10-24
related: [projects, integrations]
---

GitHub integration has three parts: sign-in (optional), import and push. All of them need the operator to configure a GitHub OAuth app; when it is missing, the GitHub panel shows a **not configured** state.

## Connect your account

1. Open [/connect-github](/connect-github) or the project's GitHub panel.
2. Authorize the Codexa OAuth app. Codexa requests repository scope so it can read and push; the token is encrypted at rest.
3. The connection is tied to your workspace and can be removed from Integrations.

## Import a repository

1. [/import-project](/import-project) → choose a repository and a branch.
2. Codexa downloads a tarball of that branch and stores the files in a new project. Git history is **not** imported; the project starts from a clean snapshot of the branch.
3. Files above the per-project storage limit are rejected with a clear message before anything is written.

Imported projects behave like template projects. The template family is detected from the files (`vite.config.*`, `package.json` scripts, or plain HTML) and determines the dev and build commands.

## Commit and push

From the GitHub panel:

1. Enter a commit message and (optionally) a branch name; the default is the branch you imported from.
2. Codexa creates a commit containing the current project files on top of the branch head and pushes it through the GitHub API.
3. The panel shows the commit link or GitHub's error message.

Push replaces the tracked files with the project's current files. It does not merge, so if the branch moved on GitHub since the import, push to a new branch and open a pull request there.

## Status

`GET /github/status` (and the panel) report whether the project is linked, the repository, the branch, and when it was last pushed.

## What is not supported yet

- Pulling updates from GitHub into an existing project (re-import creates a new project).
- Two-way sync or webhooks from GitHub.
- GitHub sign-in without the OAuth app configured.

Integrations are **connections** stored at the workspace level and used by projects in that workspace. Admins and owners manage them from the workspace's Integrations page; the [integrations directory](/integrations) lists every provider and what Codexa does with it.

## Providers

| Provider            | What the connection enables                                                     |
| ------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| GitHub              | Import a repository into a project; commit and push project files back. OAuth. |
| PostgreSQL          | Schema browser and SQL runner in projects; connection string for your code.     |
| Supabase            | Same as PostgreSQL, using the Supabase connection string.                       |
| OpenAI / Anthropic  | Credentials tested with a small request. The platform-level key configured by the operator is what the agent uses today. |
| Stripe              | Secret key stored for projects that need it; tested by reading the account.     |
| Razorpay            | Key id + secret; tested by reading the account.                                 |
| Resend              | API key for transactional email from your apps; tested by listing domains.      |
| Vercel              | Deployment token used by the Vercel deployment adapter.                         |

## Adding a connection

1. Workspace → **Integrations** → choose a provider.
2. Give it a name and paste the credential. Secrets are encrypted with the platform's encryption key before they are written to the database and are never returned by the API (`GET` responses show masked values only).
3. **Test connection** runs a provider-specific, read-only request and shows the real outcome, including the provider's error message when it fails.

A failed test does not delete the connection; fix the credential and test again.

## Using a connection in a project

Connections are not injected automatically. To use a credential in your running code, add it as a project [environment variable](/docs/environment-variables). Database connections are selectable in the Database panel; GitHub connections are used by the GitHub panel; Vercel tokens are used by the Deploy panel.

## When a provider is not configured

Some integrations also depend on operator-level configuration (for example GitHub OAuth needs a client id and secret on the server). When that is missing, the corresponding panel renders a **not configured** state with the environment variables the operator has to set, instead of a broken button.

## Removing a connection

Deleting a connection revokes it for every project in the workspace immediately. Secrets are removed with the row.

A project is the unit everything else attaches to: files, snapshots, activity, environment variables, AI conversations, runtimes and deployments. Projects belong to a workspace and inherit its members and roles.

## Creating projects

Projects start from a **template** or a **GitHub import**.

- Templates are starter codebases in three families: React + Vite + TypeScript + Tailwind single-page apps, static HTML/CSS/JS sites, and Node + Express REST APIs. Browse them at [/templates](/templates). A Next.js full-stack template is on the [roadmap](/roadmap) and is not available yet.
- GitHub import copies a repository branch into a new project once GitHub is connected. See [GitHub](/docs/github).

The number of active projects per workspace is limited by plan (3 on Free, 25 on Pro, 100 on Team). Creating one beyond the limit returns `quota_exceeded`.

## Files

Files are stored in Codexa's database (Cloudflare D1), not on a disk you can see. The file explorer, search (`Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+F`) and the agent's tools all operate on this stored copy; a running sandbox receives a synced copy of it.

- Paths are relative to the project root and may not contain `..` segments.
- A file can be up to 1 MB and a project can hold up to 2,000 files. Binary files are supported for small assets; large media belongs in object storage or a CDN.
- Deleting a folder deletes every file under it. Deletions are recorded in activity and recoverable from a snapshot taken before the deletion.

Storage per workspace is metered against the plan's limit (250 MB on Free).

## Snapshots

A snapshot is a named checkpoint of every file in the project. Its contents are stored in Cloudflare R2; the database keeps the snapshot's name, file count and size.

- Create one from the History panel with a name and optional message.
- The agent creates one automatically before each run, named `Before AI run <id>`.
- Opening a snapshot shows a per-file diff against the current files.
- **Restore** replaces the current files with the snapshot's. Restoring is itself recorded, and the state before the restore is kept as a new snapshot, so nothing is lost.

Snapshots are the mechanism behind "review and revert" for AI runs; see [AI agent](/docs/ai-agent#review-and-revert).

## Activity history

The Activity tab lists notable events with actor and time: file saves, renames, deletions, snapshots and restores, AI runs, runtime starts, deployments and settings changes. It is read-only.

## Share links

Editors and above can create a share link with `view` or `edit` access and an optional expiry in days. Anyone with the link can open the project at that level without being a workspace member. Revoke a link from the Share panel; revoked links stop working immediately.

> Warning: An `edit` share link lets anyone holding it change files and run the agent against your quota. Prefer `view` links and short expiries.

## Project settings

- **Name and description** – shown in the dashboard and in the agent's context.
- **Visibility** – private by default. Public projects can appear in the [showcase](/showcase) when you opt in.
- **Environment variables** – see [Environment variables](/docs/environment-variables).
- **Duplicate** – copies files and environment variable *names* (not values) into a new project in the same workspace.
- **Delete** – a soft delete by an owner or admin. Deleted projects are not shown and their storage is released after the retention window described in [data retention](/data-retention).

## Concurrent editing

Codexa shows presence (who has which file open) in real time. Two people editing the same file at the same time are *not* merged: the last save wins. Conflict-free collaborative editing is on the roadmap.

title: Prompting
description: Practical prompt patterns that produce maintainable code from the Codexa agent, with examples.
category: Start here

The agent edits real files with real tools. The quality of what it writes depends far more on *what you ask for* than on the model. These patterns come from the way the agent is built: it loads limited context, works in bounded steps and validates with a type-check and build.

## State the outcome, not the keystrokes

Describe the behaviour the user should see. Let the agent pick file names and implementation unless you care.

```text
Bad:  Open App.tsx and add a useState for the modal and a button that sets it.
Good: Add a "Contact us" modal that opens from the header button, traps
      focus, closes on Escape, and submits name/email/message to
      POST /api/contact.
```

## One change per run

Runs are bounded (at most 40 tool calls and 2 repair attempts). A prompt that asks for a dashboard, authentication *and* a billing page usually ends with a half-finished third item. Split it:

1. "Add the dashboard layout with a sidebar and three placeholder panels."
2. "Fill the first panel with a table of recent orders loaded from `/api/orders`."
3. "Add client-side filtering by status to that table."

Each run gets its own snapshot and diff, so reviewing is easier too.

## Name the constraints that matter

The agent reads your files, but it does not know your intentions. Say them:

```text
Add a settings page. Constraints:
- reuse the existing <Card> and <Button> components in src/components/ui
- keep all strings in src/i18n/en.ts
- no new dependencies
```

"No new dependencies" is worth saying explicitly on small projects; the sandbox will install anything in `package.json`, but you may not want it.

## Paste the error, not a description of it

In **Fix** mode, paste the exact output from the Logs panel or the build. The agent runs the same commands in the sandbox and compares.

```text
Fix this build error:

src/pages/Orders.tsx(42,18): error TS2339: Property 'total' does not exist
on type 'Order'.
```

## Use Ask mode to understand before changing

**Ask** mode gives the agent read-only tools. Use it to get an explanation of a file or an approach, then switch to **Build** with a precise request.

```text
Ask: How is form validation done in this project, and where would a new
"phone" field be validated?
```

## Give acceptance criteria for anything non-trivial

A checklist turns into tests the agent can run, or at least into things it checks before calling `finish`.

```text
Add CSV export to the orders table.
Done when:
- a "Download CSV" button appears next to the filters
- the file includes the currently filtered rows only
- dates are ISO 8601
- `npm run build` passes
```

## When to write code yourself

The editor is always there. Small renames, copy changes and one-line fixes are faster by hand and cost nothing from your AI quota. Save, and the agent will see the new content on its next run.

## What does not help

- Asking for "best practices" or "clean code" without saying which practices.
- Very long prompts that restate the whole project. The agent already reads your files; the prompt limit is 8,000 characters for a reason.
- Asking the agent to deploy, change billing or manage members. Those are product actions outside its tools; use the panels.

title: Security
description: How Codexa isolates project runtimes, protects secrets and sessions, authorizes every request, and what it does not claim.
category: Account

This page describes the security model as implemented. For the public commitments and how to report an issue, see [/security](/security) and [responsible disclosure](/responsible-disclosure).

## Runtime isolation

Generated and user code never runs inside the web application. The **runner service** executes it in a sandbox.

On Codexa's hosted service, each project runs in **its own Cloudflare Container**, a separate lightweight virtual machine owned by a Durable Object for that project:

- one project per container, so the container is the isolation boundary between projects,
- commands run as an unprivileged user inside it, with wall-clock timeouts,
- the container's instance type caps CPU, memory and disk,
- it starts on demand and stops after 30 minutes without requests,
- it has outbound internet access so dependency installs work.

In every setup:

- allow-listed commands only (`install`, `build`, `test`, `typecheck`, the template's dev command); the agent cannot run arbitrary shell,
- previews are reached through a host-based proxy that maps one preview address to one project's sandbox; sandboxes cannot see each other.

Operators who run the runner themselves get a different default driver: an unprivileged user inside Linux user, PID, mount and network namespaces, with cgroup limits on memory and process count. Optional Docker and E2B drivers are available for container or remote isolation.

## Secrets

- Environment variable values, integration credentials and GitHub tokens are encrypted with the platform encryption key before they are stored.
- The API returns masked values; revealing a value requires the editor role and is logged.
- Secrets are never included in logs, AI context or tool outputs.
- Password hashes, session tokens and email tokens are stored hashed.

## Sessions and authorization

- Sessions are httpOnly cookies backed by hashed tokens with expiry.
- Every API route authenticates the user and checks workspace role or project access on the server; client-supplied ids are never trusted.
- Admin pages require a staff account.
- Auth and AI endpoints are rate limited.

## AI boundaries

- The agent only sees file contents, the file tree, recent messages and sanitized tool output; never environment variable values.
- Paths are validated so tools cannot escape the project.
- Runs are bounded in tool calls, turns, time and tokens, and start with a snapshot so changes are reversible.
- Prompts and file contents are sent to the configured provider (Anthropic or OpenAI). The [AI policy](/ai-policy) describes this in user-facing terms.

## Webhooks

Stripe and Razorpay webhooks are verified by signature and deduplicated by event id. See [Webhooks](/api/webhooks).

## What we do not claim

Codexa has **no third-party certifications or audits** (no SOC 2, ISO 27001, HIPAA or similar) at this stage. Statements about compliance programmes will only appear here when they are true.

> Review: Public security and compliance statements beyond this engineering description require legal and security review before publication.

## Reporting a vulnerability

Email [security@codexa.app](mailto:security@codexa.app) or use the [vulnerability reporting](/vulnerability-reporting) form.

title: Troubleshooting
description: The error codes Codexa returns (quota_exceeded, ai_not_configured, runner unavailable, confirmation_required, email_taken, invalid_token, rate_limited) and what to do about each.
category: Account
order: 32
tags: [errors, troubleshooting, support]
author: Codexa Team
date: 2026-10-24
related: [ai-agent, billing, deployment]
---

Every API error has the same shape, and the product surfaces the `code` in its error messages:

```json
{ "error": { "code": "quota_exceeded", "message": "…", "details": { } } }
```

## `quota_exceeded` (402)

A plan limit was reached: AI requests or tokens, runtime minutes, deployments, storage, projects or members. `details.kind` says which. Wait for the monthly reset, free up resources (delete projects, reduce storage) or upgrade under Workspace → Billing. See [Billing](/docs/billing).

## `ai_not_configured` (503)

No AI provider key is configured on this Codexa deployment, so the agent cannot run. The agent panel shows the same state. The operator needs to set an Anthropic or OpenAI key on the server; nothing you can do in the UI changes this.

## Runner unavailable

Previews, builds and the agent's validation step need the runner service. When it is down or unreachable, `GET /runtime` reports `runnerAvailable: false`, the Preview panel shows **Runner unavailable** and runtime starts fail with a 503. The web app, editor and snapshots keep working. Check [status](/status) and try again; if it persists, contact support with the project id.

## `confirmation_required` (409)

The SQL runner refused a destructive statement (`INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`, `DROP`, `TRUNCATE`, `ALTER`) on the first attempt. Re-run with the confirmation flag (the panel asks you) if you really mean it. See [Databases](/docs/databases).

## `email_taken` (409)

An account with that email already exists. Sign in instead, or use **Forgot password** if you do not remember the password.

## `invalid_token` (400)

A verification or password-reset link is invalid, already used or expired. Request a new one from [/forgot-password](/forgot-password) or **Resend verification** on the sign-in page. Links are single-use.

## `invalid_credentials` (401)

Wrong email or password. After repeated failures the sign-in endpoint rate-limits the address.

## `rate_limited` (429)

Too many requests from your IP or account in a short window. The response includes `Retry-After` in seconds and `resetAt`. Public forms allow 5 submissions per 15 minutes; search allows 120 requests per minute; auth and AI endpoints have their own windows.

## `unauthorized` (401) / `forbidden` (403)

Your session has expired (sign in again) or your role in the workspace does not allow the action (ask an admin to change it). Viewers cannot edit, run or deploy.

## `not_found` (404)

The project, snapshot, run or workspace does not exist or you do not have access to it. Codexa deliberately does not distinguish the two cases.

## `bad_request` (400)

The request body failed validation. `details` lists each field and message. In the UI this appears as inline form errors.

## Preview does not start

1. Open the Logs panel; the sandbox's `stdout`/`stderr` is streamed there with the real error.
2. Common causes: a missing dependency (run **install**), a port other than the template's default, or a failing dev command. Fix in the editor or paste the log into a **Fix** mode prompt.
3. Runtime minutes may be exhausted (`quota_exceeded` with `kind: runtime_minutes`).

## Build fails on deploy

The build log in the Deploy panel is the complete output of the build command. Type errors stop the build; run **typecheck** before deploying, or ask the agent to fix the errors.

## Still stuck

Open a ticket at [/support](/support) with the project id, the error code and the time. Security issues go to [security@codexa.app](mailto:security@codexa.app).

Apps that call a model have one hard rule: the provider key stays on a server. This guide builds a small chat app as a Vite + React frontend plus a Node + Express API, the same split Codexa uses internally.

## Step 1: Store the credential

Add an OpenAI or Anthropic connection under workspace Integrations so it is tested, then add the key to the API project as `OPENAI_API_KEY` or `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`. Never add it to the frontend project; `VITE_*` variables end up in the public bundle.

## Step 2: The API

Create a **Node + Express** project and ask the agent:

```text
Add POST /chat that takes { messages: [{ role, content }] }, calls the
provider using the official SDK already in package.json (openai or
@anthropic-ai/sdk) and streams the reply as server-sent events:
  event: text   data: {"delta": "..."}
  event: done   data: {"inputTokens": n, "outputTokens": n}
  event: error  data: {"message": "..."}
Limit messages to 20 and each content to 4,000 characters; return 400 otherwise.
Add a per-IP rate limit of 30 requests per 15 minutes.
```

If the SDK is not in `package.json`, say "add the openai package" explicitly; the sandbox installs from the registry.

## Step 3: The frontend

```text
Add a chat UI that posts to import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL + "/chat" and
renders streamed text as it arrives (parse SSE from fetch's body stream).
Show a "not configured" message when the API returns 503.
```

## Step 4: Fail honestly when there is no key

Have the API return `503 { error: { code: "ai_not_configured" } }` when the key is missing, and have the UI show that state. Mock output for a demo is tempting and misleading; Codexa itself refuses to pretend the agent works without a key.

## Step 5: Testing without real calls

Ask the agent for a provider interface with a `MockProvider` used when `AI_MOCK=1`, so `npm test` runs in the sandbox without network access or keys. Keep the mock's output clearly labelled.

## Step 6: Cost and abuse controls

- Count tokens from the provider's usage fields and store them per user.
- Cap tokens per day per user in the API, returning 402 with a clear code.
- Keep the system prompt on the server; clients send only user messages.

## Deploy

Frontend to Codexa hosting; API to a Node host via GitHub push. Set the key only in the production API environment.

description: Structure a multi-tenant SaaS on Codexa - a React frontend, a Node + Express API, email/password auth, workspaces and Stripe or Razorpay billing.

Codexa's templates are single-purpose: a browser app, a static site or an API. A SaaS needs the first and the third. This guide builds them as two projects in the same workspace and wires them together.

## Architecture

```text
┌──────────────────┐   fetch /api/*   ┌──────────────────────┐   SQL   ┌────────────┐
│ frontend project │ ───────────────▶ │ api project (Express) │ ──────▶ │ PostgreSQL │
│ Vite + React     │                  │ sessions, tenants     │         │ (yours)    │
└──────────────────┘                  └──────────────────────┘         └────────────┘
```

The frontend deploys to Codexa hosting (static). The API runs in a preview during development and is hosted on a Node host of your choice for production; Codexa hosting is static only. See [Deployment](/docs/deployment).

## Step 1: The API project

1. Create a project from the **Node + Express** template; name it `saas-api`.
2. [Connect a database](/guides/connect-a-database) and add `DATABASE_URL` as an environment variable.
3. Ask the agent, in Build mode:

```text
Set up the data model for a multi-tenant SaaS with pg:
- tables: users, workspaces, memberships(role: owner|member), sessions
- a migrations/ folder with SQL files and an `npm run migrate` script
- bcrypt password hashing; httpOnly session cookie; requireUser middleware
- routes: POST /auth/signup, /auth/login, /auth/logout, GET /me,
  POST /workspaces, GET /workspaces
- every workspace route checks membership server-side
Done when `npm run typecheck` and `npm run build` pass.
```

4. Run the preview and use the Logs panel to confirm the server starts. Run the migration with **Run command → test** if you wired it there, or from your machine against the same database.

## Step 2: The frontend project

1. Create a project from a **Vite + React** template; name it `saas-web`.
2. Add `VITE_API_URL` as an environment variable pointing at the API preview URL.
3. Ask the agent:

```text
Add sign-up, sign-in and a workspace switcher that talk to the API at
import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL with credentials: "include".
Protected routes redirect to /login when GET /me returns 401.
```

> Note: Cookies across two origins need the API to send `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials` and `SameSite=None; Secure` in production. Ask the agent to add the CORS configuration with the frontend origin from an environment variable.

## Step 3: Billing

Add a Stripe (international) or Razorpay (India) connection under workspace Integrations so the credential is tested, then add the secret as `STRIPE_SECRET_KEY` or `RAZORPAY_KEY_ID`/`RAZORPAY_KEY_SECRET` in the API project.

```text
Add subscription billing with Stripe Checkout:
- POST /billing/checkout creates a Checkout session for the current workspace
- POST /webhooks/stripe verifies the signature, stores event ids in a
  webhook_events table and ignores duplicates, and updates
  workspaces.plan on checkout.session.completed and
  customer.subscription.deleted
- never trust plan changes from the client
```

That is the same pattern Codexa uses for its own billing: verify, deduplicate, then act. See [Webhooks](/api/webhooks).

## Step 4: Enforce limits server-side

Whatever your plans promise, check them in the API before the action happens, and return a consistent error. Codexa returns `402 quota_exceeded`; copying that shape keeps the frontend simple.

## Step 5: Deploy

- `saas-web` → Codexa hosting, with `VITE_API_URL` set to the production API URL at build time.
- `saas-api` → push to GitHub from the GitHub panel and deploy to your Node host; point `DATABASE_URL` and the session secret at production values there.

## Checklist before launch

- Passwords hashed, sessions httpOnly, CORS restricted to your origin.
- Every workspace route checks membership.
- Webhook signature verified and events deduplicated.
- Environment variables set in both projects; none committed to GitHub.

2. Name it, paste the connection string, and press **Test**. The test runs `SELECT 1` and shows the real driver error when it fails (wrong password, unreachable host, SSL required).

> Tip: For Supabase, copy the **transaction pooler** URL from the project's database settings and append `?sslmode=require` if your driver needs it.

## Step 2: Browse the schema

Open any project's **Database** panel and select the connection. Tables, columns, types, keys and indexes are read live. Nothing is cached, so changes made elsewhere show up immediately.

## Step 3: Run SQL

Use the SQL runner for exploration:

```sql
select table_name, column_name, data_type
from information_schema.columns
where table_schema = 'public'
order by table_name, ordinal_position;
```

Destructive statements ask for confirmation on the first attempt (`confirmation_required`). That is intentional; read [Databases](/docs/databases#sql-runner).

In a Node + Express project, add `DATABASE_URL` under **Settings → Environment variables**, restart the preview, and ask the agent:

```text
Add a pg Pool created from process.env.DATABASE_URL and a GET /api/health
route that runs `select now()` and returns the timestamp.
```

Open `/api/health` in the preview to confirm the round trip.

## Step 5: Migrations

Create a `migrations/` folder with numbered SQL files and an npm script that applies them in order. Run it from **Run command** or your own machine. Codexa does not run migrations automatically; that keeps surprises out of production.

A Vite + React app must not hold a database password. Put the queries behind an Express project, or use Supabase row-level security with the anon key.

title: Fix a failing build with Fix mode
description: Introduce a type error on purpose, watch the sandbox catch it, and let the agent repair it within its two-attempt limit.

The agent's repair loop is easiest to understand when you break something yourself first.

## 1. Break the build

Open any Vite + React project. In `src/App.tsx` add:

```ts
const count: number = "three";
```

Save with `Ctrl/Cmd+S`. Monaco underlines the line immediately, but the authoritative check is the sandbox.

## 2. Run the real type-check

Logs panel → **Run command → typecheck**. The output is the real `tsc` result:

```text
src/App.tsx(4,7): error TS2322: Type 'string' is not assignable to type 'number'.
```

## 3. Hand it to Fix mode

Switch the agent to **Fix** and paste the error verbatim. Fix mode uses the same tools as Build with a repair-oriented prompt. Watch the stages:

- `loading_context` reads `src/App.tsx` because the error names it.
- `planning` proposes a one-line change.
- `working` edits the file (a snapshot is created first).
- `validating` runs `typecheck` again and gets a clean result.

## 4. See the bound

If a fix introduces a new error, the agent enters `repairing` and tries again, at most twice. After that the run ends as `failed` with the last error shown, and the snapshot lets you revert. This is deliberate: an unbounded loop would burn your quota on a problem that needs a human.

## 5. Review

Open the run in History and inspect the diff. It should touch one line. If the agent did more than you asked, that is a sign the prompt was too open; see [Prompting](/docs/prompting).

Restyle the header: dark background, centered logo, uppercase navigation.

- The state before the revert is itself saved as a snapshot, so a revert is reversible too.

Before a large request, create a snapshot manually with a meaningful name ("before pricing page"). Automatic snapshots are per run; yours can span several.

---
title: How the sandbox isolates your project
description: Generated code never runs inside Codexa's web server. A look at the runner service, one Cloudflare Container per project, the self-hosted drivers and the preview proxy.
category: Engineering
tags: [sandbox, security, runtime]
author: Codexa Team
date: 2026-10-24
updated: 2026-10-27
related: [why-codexa-snapshots-before-every-ai-run]
---

The first rule we wrote down for Codexa was that user code, and code written by a model, never executes in the same process as the web application. Everything that runs, from `npm install` to a dev server, runs in a sandbox managed by a separate service. This post describes that service as it exists today.

> Note: Updated 27 October 2026. Since [release 0.2.0](/changelog/cloudflare-platform), Codexa's hosted service runs the runner inside one Cloudflare Container per project. The section "On Cloudflare: one container per project" below describes that setup. The namespace and cgroup sandbox described after it is what a self-hosted runner uses by default.

## Two processes, one job each

The **web app** stores files, authenticates people, talks to the AI provider and renders the UI. It cannot spawn a shell.

The **runner** is a separate Node service with one job: given a project id and an allow-listed command, materialise the files into an isolated working directory, run the command with limits, and stream the output back. The web app talks to it over an authenticated internal API; the runner trusts nothing from the browser.

## On Cloudflare: one container per project

On the hosted service, every project gets its own Cloudflare Container: a separate lightweight virtual machine, owned by a Durable Object for that project. The runner inside it holds exactly one project, so the container itself is the boundary between projects.

- Commands run as an unprivileged user, with a wall-clock timeout on each one.
- The container's instance type caps CPU, memory and disk.
- It starts on demand (a preview, Run, a command or a build) and stops after 30 minutes without requests.
- It has outbound internet access, so `npm install` can fetch custom dependencies.

## Self-hosted: what "isolated" means there

When an operator runs the runner on their own machine, the default driver runs each command as an unprivileged user inside fresh Linux namespaces:

- a **user namespace** so root inside is nobody outside,
- a **PID namespace** so the process tree cannot see or signal anything else,
- a **mount namespace** with the project directory and a read-only toolchain,
- a **network namespace** with the policy the operator chooses for package installs.

Resource limits come from **cgroups**: a memory ceiling, a process count ceiling, and a wall-clock timeout on every command. Hitting a limit kills the command and the log says so; it does not take the host with it.

Operators who prefer containers can switch to the **Docker** driver, and those who want execution off the box entirely can use the **E2B** driver. The web app does not know or care which one is active.

## Commands are allow-listed

The agent's `run_command` tool and the Logs panel can run exactly `install`, `build`, `test` and `typecheck`, plus the template's dev command for previews. There is no "run arbitrary shell" tool. That removes a whole category of prompt-injection outcomes: a malicious README cannot talk the model into exfiltrating anything, because the tool to do so does not exist.

## Previews without opening ports

A running preview listens on a port inside its sandbox. Users reach it through a **host-based proxy**: each sandbox gets a hostname, the proxy maps the hostname to the sandbox, and nothing else is reachable. Sandboxes do not see each other's hostnames or networks. On Cloudflare, the Worker forwards each preview address to that project's container.

## Logs are the truth

Every line of `stdout` and `stderr` is streamed to the Logs panel and to the agent when it asks. We do not summarise or hide errors, because the next step (yours or the agent's) depends on the real message.

## What this does not claim

Isolation of this kind is a strong engineering boundary, not a certification. Codexa has not been audited by a third party, and we say so on the [security page](/docs/security). If you find a way out of the sandbox, we want to know: [security@codexa.app](mailto:security@codexa.app).

title: Prompting patterns that produce maintainable code
description: Five habits that turn a code-writing agent from a slot machine into a colleague, learned from building and using Codexa's own agent.
category: Practice
tags: [prompting, ai, best-practices]
author: Codexa Team
date: 2026-10-24
related: [why-codexa-snapshots-before-every-ai-run]
---

The Codexa agent has a small set of tools, a bounded loop and a validation step. Within those bounds the biggest variable is the prompt. These are the patterns that consistently gave us code we were happy to keep.

## 1. Describe behaviour, let the agent choose structure

"Add a modal that opens from the header button, traps focus and closes on Escape" produces better code than "add a useState and a div". The model knows how to build a modal; it does not know what you want the modal to do.

## 2. One concern per run

The repair loop is capped at two attempts, and a run that tries to do three things usually fails on the third. Three runs of one thing each are cheaper, faster to review and easier to revert individually.

## 3. Say the constraints you care about

- "No new dependencies."
- "Reuse the components in `src/components/ui`."
- "Keep strings in the i18n file."

These sentences are cheap and prevent the most common complaint about generated code: it is fine, but it does not look like the rest of the project.

## 4. Write acceptance criteria

A "done when" list becomes something the agent checks before it calls `finish`, and something you check in the diff. If you cannot write the criteria, the request is not ready.

## 5. Use Ask mode before Build mode on unfamiliar code

Read-only tools, no writes. "How is validation done here and where would a phone field go?" costs little and makes the Build prompt precise.

## Two anti-patterns

- **Restating the project.** The agent already reads your files. Long prompts that describe the codebase waste the 8,000-character budget and add nothing.
- **Asking for virtues.** "Make it clean and follow best practices" is not actionable. Name the practice.

## Why this matters more with an agent than with autocomplete

Autocomplete suggests a line you were about to write. An agent writes files you have not seen. The prompt is the only place your intent lives, so it has to carry the constraints you would otherwise enforce while typing. The [prompting guide](/docs/prompting) has more examples.

---
title: Why Codexa snapshots before every AI run
description: An AI that edits real files needs an undo button that always works. Here is how snapshots make every agent run reviewable and reversible.
category: Engineering
tags: [ai, snapshots, design]
author: Codexa Team
date: 2026-10-24
related: [how-the-sandbox-isolates-your-project]
---

An agent that can write files is only useful if you can trust it to be wrong sometimes. We spent more time on the undo path than on the generation path, and this post explains why and how.

## The problem with "apply this diff"

Many tools show a proposed change and ask you to accept it. That works for one file. It stops working when a change touches eight files, adds a dependency and rewrites a config, because the question "do I accept this?" is really "do I understand all of this?", and the honest answer is often no.

We wanted a different question: **can I get back to where I was, exactly, in one click?** If the answer is always yes, you can let the agent work, look at the result, and decide afterwards.

## What a snapshot is

A snapshot in Codexa is a named checkpoint of every file in the project, stored in the same database as the files. Snapshots are cheap: files are content-addressed, so a snapshot of a project where one file changed stores one new blob and a list of references.

The agent takes one automatically, named `Before AI run <id>`, at the moment it is about to make its first write. Not when the run starts (a run that only reads should not litter your history) and not at the end (too late to be useful if the run is cancelled).

## What you get from it

- **A real diff.** Opening a run shows each changed file against the snapshot, not against a guess about what the agent "meant" to change.
- **Revert in one click.** Restoring the snapshot replaces the current files. The state before the restore is saved as a new snapshot, so even the revert is reversible.
- **Cancel without fear.** If you cancel a run mid-way, files already written stay, but the snapshot is there. Partial runs are not scary.

## The limits that make it work

Snapshots are necessary but not sufficient. The agent is also bounded: at most 40 tool calls, 60 model turns, 25 minutes and two repair attempts per run. A bounded run produces a bounded diff, which is the kind a person can actually review. An unbounded agent produces changes nobody reads.

## What we did not build

We did not build "accept hunk by hunk". If you want part of a run, edit by hand or ask for a follow-up; both take a few seconds and keep the model simple. We also did not build automatic acceptance based on tests passing. Passing tests are evidence, not consent.

## Trying it

Open any project, ask for something you are not sure about, and look for the snapshot in the History panel. The [tutorial](/tutorials/review-and-revert-an-ai-run) walks through review and revert.

## "GitHub is not configured"

The operator has not set up a GitHub OAuth app on this deployment. Import and push are unavailable until they do; everything else works.

## Importing a repository

[/import-project](/import-project) → pick a repository and branch. Files are copied into a new project; git history is not. Repositories larger than your plan's storage limit are refused before anything is written.

## Pushing changes

GitHub panel → commit message → **Push**. Codexa creates a commit with the project's current files on the chosen branch. If the branch changed on GitHub since you imported, push to a new branch and open a pull request.

## Push failed with a permission error

Reconnect GitHub from Integrations; the token may have been revoked, or the repository belongs to an organisation that has not approved the app.

## Pulling updates from GitHub

Not supported yet. Import again into a new project, or copy the changed files in the editor.

## What a preview is

**Run** starts your project in an isolated sandbox and exposes it at a preview URL. Dependencies are installed, the template's dev command runs, and output streams into the Logs panel.

## It will not start

1. Read the Logs panel; the real error is there.
2. **Runner unavailable** means the execution service is down. Editing and snapshots still work; try again later or check [status](/status).
3. `quota_exceeded` with `runtime_minutes` means the month's runtime allowance is used (5 hours on Free).
4. A dependency error: run **install** from the Logs panel.

## Runtime minutes

Minutes are counted while a sandbox is running, whether or not you are looking at it. Previews stop automatically after a period of inactivity and when you press **Stop**. The Usage page shows the running total.

## Changes do not show up

Saved files are synced into the running sandbox. If the dev server needs a restart (for example after changing environment variables), press **Restart**.

## Sharing a preview URL

Preview URLs are tied to the sandbox and your session; they are not public hosting. To share something durable, [deploy](/help/deployments) it.

## How many projects can I have?

Free: 3, Pro: 25, Team: 100 active projects per workspace. Deleted projects do not count. Over the limit, creating a project returns `quota_exceeded`.

## Which templates exist?

React + Vite + TypeScript + Tailwind apps, static HTML/CSS/JS sites and Node + Express APIs. A Next.js template is on the roadmap. Browse [/templates](/templates).

## I lost changes

Open the History panel. Every agent run and every manual snapshot is a full checkpoint; restoring one brings files back. Restores are themselves snapshotted, so you can undo an undo.

## Sharing a project

Share panel → create a link with `view` or `edit` access and an optional expiry. Revoke links from the same panel. Workspace members do not need links.

## Duplicating

Project menu → **Duplicate** copies the files into a new project in the same workspace. Environment variable names are copied; values are not.

## Deleting and recovering

Deleting is a soft delete by an owner or admin. [Contact support](/help/contacting-support) within the retention window described in [data retention](/data-retention) to recover one.

## Two people edited the same file

Last save wins. Codexa shows who is viewing each file, but concurrent editing with merging is not available yet. Use snapshots to recover an overwritten version.

## Creating a team workspace

Workspace switcher → **New workspace**. Team workspaces are available on the Team plan (up to 10 members) and Enterprise.

## Roles

Viewer (read), Editor (edit, run, deploy), Admin (members, integrations), Owner (billing, delete). Details in [getting started](/docs/getting-started#workspaces).

## Inviting someone

Workspace → **Members** → **Invite** with an email and role. The invitee gets an email and must sign in with that address. Invitations expire; resend from the same page.

## Changing roles and removing members

Admins and owners change roles from the Members page. Removing a member revokes their access immediately; their past activity is kept in the log.

## Transferring ownership

The current owner can promote an admin to owner; there is exactly one owner per workspace.

## Working on the same file

Presence shows who has a file open. Simultaneous edits are not merged; the last save wins. Coordinate on shared files or use snapshots to recover.

Release **0.2.0** moves the whole hosted service onto Cloudflare. Email is the one exception: account emails go through Customer.io. Features work as they did in 0.1.0; this entry lists where each part now runs and what changed as a result.

## Database on D1

- Accounts, workspaces, projects, project files, billing records and jobs live in Cloudflare D1 (SQLite) instead of PostgreSQL.
- A file can be up to 1 MB and a project can hold up to 2,000 files. Storage is metered per workspace, as before.

## Snapshots and hosted sites on R2

- Snapshot contents are stored in Cloudflare R2. The database keeps each snapshot's name, file count and size.
- Codexa hosting builds the site in the project's container, uploads the output to R2 and serves the live deployment from the Worker. Rollback switches which deployment is live, without rebuilding.

## Runtime on Cloudflare Containers

- Each project gets its own Cloudflare Container, owned by a Durable Object. It starts on demand for a preview, Run, a command or a build, and stops after 30 minutes without requests.
- Inside the container the runner works as before: allow-listed commands only, run as an unprivileged user, with output streamed to the Logs panel. The container is the isolation boundary between projects.
- Previews are served at a per-project preview address that the Worker forwards to that project's container.

## Presence and background jobs

- "Who's online" in the editor runs on a Durable Object per project, with the same protocol as before.
- Background jobs (email retries, session and token cleanup, usage roll-ups, runtime sweeps) run from a Cron Trigger every 5 minutes.

## For operators

- `npm run setup` logs in to Cloudflare, stores the secrets, deploys and creates the database tables. `docs/CLOUDFLARE.md` in the repository is the step-by-step guide.
- Without a custom domain Codexa runs on a `workers.dev` address. Everything works except live preview, Run and Codexa hosting, and the app says plainly that those need a domain.

Documentation: [Projects](/docs/projects), [Security](/docs/security), [Deployment](/docs/deployment).

The first public release of Codexa, **0.1.0**, ships the account and API foundation that every other area builds on.

## Accounts

- Email/password sign-up with verification emails and single-use, expiring tokens.
- Password reset with the same token mechanism.
- Sessions as httpOnly cookies; session tokens stored hashed with expiry and revocation.
- GitHub sign-in when the operator configures an OAuth app; the sign-in page shows the button only in that case.
- A personal workspace for every account.

## API conventions

- All JSON endpoints under `/api/v1/*`, authentication under `/api/auth/*`, inbound webhooks under `/api/webhooks/*`.
- One error shape everywhere: `{ error: { code, message, details? } }` with 400/401/402/403/404/409/429/500.
- Every handler authenticates, checks workspace role or project access on the server, and validates bodies with zod.
- Rate limiting on auth, AI and public form endpoints with `Retry-After`.

## Operator configuration

Capabilities that depend on external services (email, GitHub, AI providers, Stripe, Razorpay, Vercel, E2B) are detected from server environment variables and rendered as explicit "not configured" states in the product when missing.

## Runner service

- A separate service (not the Next.js process) that materialises project files and runs commands.
- Default driver: unprivileged user, Linux user/PID/mount/network namespaces, cgroup memory and process limits, per-command timeouts.
- Optional Docker and E2B drivers selected by operator configuration.
- Since [0.2.0](/changelog/cloudflare-platform), Codexa's hosted service runs the runner inside one Cloudflare Container per project; the container is the isolation boundary and commands run as an unprivileged user. The drivers above remain for self-hosted runners.
- Allow-listed commands only: `install`, `build`, `test`, `typecheck` and the template's dev command.

## Previews

- Start/stop a runtime per project; `GET /runtime` reports the session and whether the runner is reachable.
- Host-based proxy mapping one hostname to one sandbox.
- Logs streamed over SSE (`stdout`, `stderr`, `system`) into the Logs panel.
- File sync from the editor into the running sandbox.
- Viewport controls for phone, tablet and desktop widths.
- Runtime minutes metered against the plan.
